claim: There is growing evidence for a coupling of actin assembly and myosin motor activity in cells.
source: There is growing evidence for a coupling of actin assembly and myosin motor activity in cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, supported by the subsequent citations and discussion in the manuscript.

claim: Mechanisms for recruitment of actin nucleators and motors on specific membrane compartments remain unclear.
source: However, mechanisms for recruitment of actin nucleators and motors on specific membrane compartments remain unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: The myosin V globular tail domain (MyoV-GTD) interacts directly with an evolutionarily conserved Spir sequence motif.
source: The myosin V globular tail domain (MyoV-GTD) interacts directly with an evolutionarily conserved Spir sequence motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental approaches including co-IP, GST-pulldown, and structural studies.

claim: Crystal structures of MyoVa-GTD bound either to the Spir-2 motif or to Rab11 were determined.
source: We determined crystal structures of MyoVa-GTD bound either to the Spir-2 motif or to Rab11
evidence: The manuscript reports solving these crystal structures, with data collection and refinement statistics provided in Table 1.

claim: A Spir-2:MyoVa:Rab11 complex can form.
source: We determined crystal structures of MyoVa-GTD bound either to the Spir-2 motif or to Rab11 and show that a Spir-2:MyoVa:Rab11 complex can form.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches including analytical gel filtration, GST-pulldown assays, and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The ternary complex architecture explains how Rab11 vesicles support coordinated F-actin nucleation and myosin force generation for vesicle transport and tethering.
source: The ternary complex architecture explains how Rab11 vesicles support coordinated F-actin nucleation and myosin force generation for vesicle transport and tethering.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MyoV binds several Rab GTPases.
source: Since MyoV binds several Rab GTPases, synchronized nucleator and motor targeting could provide a common mechanism to control force generation and motility in different cellular processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (e.g., Bultema et al., 2014; Lindsay et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2011) mentioned in the Discussion.

claim: Cooperation of class I myosin with the actin nucleator Arp2/3 complex is required for membrane remodeling in endocytosis.
source: For example, the cooperation of class I myosin with the actin nucleator Arp2/3 complex is required for membrane remodeling in endocytosis (Cheng et al., 2012; Sirotkin et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: In mouse oocytes, actin nucleators Spir and formin-2 (FMN2) cooperate to generate actin filaments at Rab11 vesicle membranes.
source: In mouse oocytes, actin nucleators Spir and formin-2 (FMN2) cooperate to generate actin filaments at Rab11 vesicle membranes, while myosin Vb (MyoVb) mediates the Rab11 vesicle long-range transport towards the oocyte cortex at metaphase (Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: MyoVb mediates the Rab11 vesicle long-range transport towards the oocyte cortex at metaphase in mouse oocytes.
source: In mouse oocytes, actin nucleators Spir and formin-2 (FMN2) cooperate to generate actin filaments at Rab11 vesicle membranes, while myosin Vb (MyoVb) mediates the Rab11 vesicle long-range transport towards the oocyte cortex at metaphase (Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Nucleus positioning in mouse oocytes results from myosin V driven active diffusion of Rab11 vesicles, which also requires Spir:formin-2 dependent actin polymerization on these membranes.
source: Moreover, nucleus positioning in mouse oocytes results from myosin V driven active diffusion of Rab11 vesicles, which also requires Spir:formin-2 dependent actin polymerization on these membranes (Ahmed et al., 2015; Almonacid et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Direct interaction between the membrane anchored active Rab11 small GTPase and MyoV (MyoVa and MyoVb) globular tail domain (GTD) is necessary to target the motor to Rab11 vesicles.
source: Direct interaction between the membrane anchored active Rab11 small GTPase and MyoV (MyoVa and MyoVb) globular tail domain (GTD) is necessary to target the motor to Rab11 vesicles (Lapierre et al., 2001; Lindsay et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: A direct interaction between Spir and Rab11 could not be detected.
source: In contrast, a direct interaction between Spir and Rab11 could not be detected and it is still unclear how differential recruitment of the motors and the actin track regulators can be specified to promote Rab11-vesicle transport.
evidence: This is a negative result that motivates the investigation of alternative mechanisms for Spir recruitment.

claim: Spir actin nucleators encode a FYVE-type zinc finger membrane-binding domain at their C-termini.
source: The Spir actin nucleators (Spir-1 and Spir-2 in mammals) encode a FYVE-type zinc finger membrane-binding domain at their C-termini (Kerkhoff et al., 2001; Otto et al., 2000; Tittel et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: The FYVE-type zinc finger of Spir promiscuously interacts with negatively charged lipids.
source: The Spir actin nucleators (Spir-1 and Spir-2 in mammals) encode a FYVE-type zinc finger membrane-binding domain at their C-termini (Kerkhoff et al., 2001; Otto et al., 2000; Tittel et al., 2015) that promiscuously interacts with negatively charged lipids (Tittel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: It has been proposed that the interaction of Spir proteins with additional factors provides the specificity for its targeting to the correct subpopulation of vesicles.
source: It has been proposed that the interaction of Spir proteins with additional factors provides the specificity for its targeting to the correct subpopulation of vesicles (Tittel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: GST-MyoVb-GTD is able to pull endogenous Spir-1 from mouse brain lysates.
source: Our initial GST-pulldown experiments showed that GST-MyoVb-GTD is able to pull endogenous Spir-1 from mouse brain lysates, as does the GST-FMN2-eFSI protein that binds directly to the Spir KIND domain (Pechlivanis et al., 2009) as a positive control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GST-pulldown experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GST-FMN2-eFSI protein binds directly to the Spir KIND domain.
source: Our initial GST-pulldown experiments showed that GST-MyoVb-GTD is able to pull endogenous Spir-1 from mouse brain lysates, as does the GST-FMN2-eFSI protein that binds directly to the Spir KIND domain (Pechlivanis et al., 2009) as a positive control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Full-length Spir-1 and Spir-2 proteins interact with the GFP-MyoVb-GTD in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: In co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments employing human embryonic kidney cells transiently over-expressing recombinant Spir and MyoV, the full-length Spir-1 and Spir-2 proteins did interact with the GFP-MyoVb-GTD (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-IP experiment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Spir central linker region is important for MyoVb-GTD binding.
source: We mapped the Spir sequences necessary for the interaction with MyoVb by successive N-terminal deletions of Spir-2. The deletion of KIND and WH2 domains did not affect complex formation; however, further deletion of the linker region between the WH2 domains and the Spir-box (Figure 1) completely impaired the interaction (Figure 2A), demonstrating that the Spir central linker region is important for MyoVb-GTD binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the deletion mapping experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The GTDs of MyoVb and MyoVa are highly conserved.
source: The GTDs of MyoVb and MyoVa are highly conserved (Pylypenko et al., 2013) and both directly interact with Rab11 (Lindsay et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Both MyoVa-GTD and MyoVb-GTD directly interact with Rab11.
source: The GTDs of MyoVb and MyoVa are highly conserved (Pylypenko et al., 2013) and both directly interact with Rab11 (Lindsay et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: GFP-MyoVa-GTD interacts with Spir-2.
source: Interestingly, GFP-MyoVa-GTD also interacts with Spir-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-IP experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MyoVa and MyoVb have overlapping cellular functions.
source: This is consistent with the fact that MyoVa and MyoVb have overlapping cellular functions (such as mobilization of Rab11 recycling endosomes for the AMPA receptor transport into dendritic spines [Correia et al., 2008; Hammer and Wagner, 2013; Wang et al., 2008]), share interacting partners and utilize similar mechanisms for Rab11-vesicle transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Both MyoVa and MyoVb bind the Spir-2-linker (aa 361–519) with similar affinities in the sub-micromolar range.
source: Further experiments showed that both MyoVa and MyoVb bind the Spir-2-linker (aa 361–519) with similar affinities in the sub-micromolar range (Kd ~ 728 nM and 377 nM for MyoVa and MyoVb, respectively) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MyoVa binds Spir-2-linker with a Kd of approximately 728 nM.
source: Further experiments showed that both MyoVa and MyoVb bind the Spir-2-linker (aa 361–519) with similar affinities in the sub-micromolar range (Kd ~ 728 nM and 377 nM for MyoVa and MyoVb, respectively) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from fluorescence spectroscopy shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MyoVb binds Spir-2-linker with a Kd of approximately 377 nM.
source: Further experiments showed that both MyoVa and MyoVb bind the Spir-2-linker (aa 361–519) with similar affinities in the sub-micromolar range (Kd ~ 728 nM and 377 nM for MyoVa and MyoVb, respectively) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from fluorescence spectroscopy shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Full-length MyoVa (eGFP-MyoVa-FL) and Spir-2 (Myc-Spir-2-FL) proteins colocalize on vesicular structures in the central cytoplasm when co-expressed in HeLa cells.
source: Transgenic co-expression of tagged full-length MyoVa (eGFP-MyoVa-FL) and Spir-2 (Myc-Spir-2-FL) proteins in HeLa cells showed a perfect colocalization of the two proteins on vesicular structures in the central cytoplasm, consistent with formation of a Spir:MyoV complex at vesicle membranes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MyoVb and Spir-2 colocalize on vesicular structures when co-expressed in HeLa cells.
source: This was also the case for MyoVb and Spir-2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FLIM-FRET microscopy experiments confirm complex formation of Spir-2 and MyoVa on vesicle membranes.
source: In order to confirm a complex formation of Spir-2 and MyoVa on vesicle membranes we performed FLIM-FRET (fluorescence life time imaging, fluorescence resonance energy transfer) microscopy experiments (Sun et al., 2013) with co-expressed AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD as a donor fluorophore and mStrawberry-Spir-2 deletion mutants as acceptor fluorophores.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FLIM-FRET experiments shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: mStrawberry-Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE is able to reduce the fluorescence lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor at vesicle membrane surfaces.
source: A mStrawberry-tagged C-terminal Spir-2 protein (mStrawberry-Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE), including the Spir-GTBM (necessary for MyoV interaction), the Spir-box and the FYVE-type zinc finger (Spir membrane interaction) is able to reduce the fluorescence lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor at vesicle membrane surfaces (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FLIM-FRET experiments shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: mStrawberry-Spir-2-SB-FYVE does not alter the lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor.
source: In contrast, a mStrawberry-fusion protein encoding only the Spir-box and the FYVE-type zinc finger (mStrawberry-Spir-2-SB-FYVE) or a mutant Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE-LALA protein, in which two essential leucines for MyoV interaction were replaced by alanines, did not alter the lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FLIM-FRET experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE-LALA protein does not alter the lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor.
source: In contrast, a mStrawberry-fusion protein encoding only the Spir-box and the FYVE-type zinc finger (mStrawberry-Spir-2-SB-FYVE) or a mutant Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE-LALA protein, in which two essential leucines for MyoV interaction were replaced by alanines, did not alter the lifetime of the AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD donor (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the FLIM-FRET experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The lifetime reduction indicates that MyoVa and Spir-2 proteins are in close proximity (within 10 nm of distance between the fluorophores).
source: As the lifetime reduction indicates that MyoVa and Spir-2 proteins are in close proximity (within 10 nm of distance between the fluorophores), these results provide a strong support for a direct interaction of the two proteins at vesicle membranes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FLIM-FRET data based on the known properties of FRET.

claim: The MyoVa-GTD is monomeric in solution.
source: The MyoVa-GTD is monomeric in solution (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analytical gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-expressed green and red-fluorescent protein tagged MyoVa-GTDs as a donor/acceptor pair revealed a similar FRET efficiency as the donor alone.
source: To exclude a FLIM-FRET signal by a dense packing of proteins at vesicle membranes, we co-expressed green and red-fluorescent protein tagged MyoVa-GTDs as a donor/acceptor pair (AcGFP-MyoVa-GTD, mStrawberry-MyoVa-GTD) which revealed a similar FRET efficiency as the donor alone (Figure 3E), indicating that a direct interaction of MyoVa-GTD and the Spir-2-GTBM is required for the observed FLIM-FRET signal.
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 3E to rule out artifacts from protein crowding.

claim: Vertebrate Spir-1 and Spir-2 proteins show low overall sequence homology in their linker regions.
source: The linker regions of vertebrate Spir-1 and Spir-2 proteins show low overall sequence homology (for example similarity 21%, identity 11% between human Spir-1 and Spir-2 linker regions) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A short sequence of 27 amino acids in the middle part of the Spir linker is more conserved (similarity 56%, identity 37%).
source: The linker regions of vertebrate Spir-1 and Spir-2 proteins show low overall sequence homology (for example similarity 21%, identity 11% between human Spir-1 and Spir-2 linker regions) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) but a short sequence of 27 amino acids (Figure 4A) in the middle part of the linker is more conserved (similarity 56%, identity 37%) suggesting that the fragment could possibly have an important role in the recruitment of MyoV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spir-2 fragments containing the fully conserved regions interact with MyoVb-GTD.
source: Interestingly, Spir-2 fragments containing the fully conserved regions interact with MyoVb-GTD, whereas no interactions were observed with fragments lacking half of this region (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of two highly conserved Spir-2 residues (Leu408Ala and Leu409Ala) is sufficient to abolish direct binding to MyoV-GTD.
source: Mutation of two highly conserved Spir-2 residues within this newly identified Spir linker homology region, Leu408Ala and Leu409Ala, is sufficient to abolish direct binding to MyoV-GTD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GST-pulldown experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The minimal MyoV globular tail domain binding motif of Spir (Spir-GTBM), corresponding to the human Spir-2 short peptide (aa 401–427) binds MyoVa and MyoVb GTDs with low micromolar affinity.
source: The identified minimal MyoV globular tail domain binding motif of Spir (Spir-GTBM), corresponding to the human Spir-2 short peptide (aa 401–427) binds MyoVa and MyoVb GTDs with low micromolar affinity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Spir-2-GTBM peptide binds to the SD-1 of the MyoVa-GTD in an extended conformation, forming a two-turn alpha helix at the end, in the cleft between helices H3 and H5.
source: The Spir-2-GTBM peptide binds to the SD-1 of the MyoVa-GTD in an extended conformation, forming a two-turn alpha helix at the end, in the cleft between helices H3 and H5 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Spir-2-GTBM can be accommodated on the surface of MyoVa without conformational changes in the GTD.
source: Spir-2-GTBM can be accommodated on the surface of MyoVa without conformational changes in the GTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The Spir-GTBM binding pocket is structurally conserved in MyoVb and MyoVc.
source: Spir-2-GTBM can be accommodated on the surface of MyoVa without conformational changes in the GTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B), and the Spir-GTBM binding pocket is structurally conserved in MyoVb and MyoVc (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparisons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: MyoVc-GTD binds Spir-2-GTBM with micromolar range affinity.
source: Consistently, a direct binding assay also showed that MyoVc-GTD binds Spir-2-GTBM with micromolar range affinity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the microscale thermophoresis measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The Spir-binding site structural conservation of the three myosin V isoforms explains Spir promiscuity in binding to MyoVa, Vb and Vc.
source: We thus conclude that the Spir-binding site structural conservation of the three myosin V isoforms explains Spir promiscuity in binding to MyoVa, Vb and Vc.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and binding data presented.

claim: The MyoV-GTD Spir-2 binding site partially overlaps with that of melanophilin (MLPH).
source: Interestingly, the MyoV-GTD Spir-2 binding site partially overlaps with that of melanophilin (MLPH) (Pylypenko et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2013) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Both Spir-2-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM bind the MyoVa-GTD with similar micromolar range affinities.
source: Both Spir-2-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM bind the MyoVa-GTD with similar micromolar range affinities (Figure 4B) (Pylypenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the binding measurements shown in Figure 4B and cited reference.

claim: In contrast to the Spir-GTBM, which interacts with all three MyoV isoforms, the MLPH-GTBM binding is MyoVa specific.
source: However, in contrast to the Spir-GTBM, which interacts with all three MyoV isoforms, the MLPH-GTBM binding is MyoVa specific (Wei et al., 2013; Pylypenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: The Spir-2 and MLPH GTBMs exhibit some sequence similarity.
source: The Spir-2 and MLPH GTBMs exhibit some sequence similarity (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The N-terminal regions of Spir-2-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM interact with MyoVa in a very similar way, forming a network of hydrogen bonds with the H4''-H5-loop.
source: The Spir-2 and MLPH GTBMs exhibit some sequence similarity (Figure 4F) and comparison of the complex structures shows that their N-terminal regions interact with MyoVa in a very similar way, forming a network of hydrogen bonds with the H4''-H5-loop and similarly positioning two conserved leucine residues of the motif (L408 and L409 in Spir-2; L188 and L189 in MLPH) within cavities of the MyoVa-GTD surface (Figure 4D,E,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4D,E,H.

claim: The apo-MyoV-GTD surface is preformed to bind Spir-GTBM.
source: The apo-MyoV-GTD surface is preformed to bind Spir-GTBM (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: MLPH-GTBM cannot be accommodated on the surface of apo-MyoVa-GTD without conformational changes.
source: In contrast to Spir-GTBM, the MLPH-GTBM cannot be accommodated on the surface of apo-MyoVa-GTD without conformational changes (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4H.

claim: MLPH-GTBM binding to MyoVa requires rotation of the Tyr1596 side chain in towards the protein core to harbor the big Phe side chain in the binding pocket.
source: MLPH-GTBM has a conserved hydrophobic residue (Phe, Ile or Val) Phe191 at the position equivalent to the Spir-2-A411 (Figure 4E,F,H) and its binding to MyoVa requires rotation of the Tyr1596 side chain in towards the protein core to harbor the big Phe side chain in the binding pocket (Figure 4H,I; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 4H,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The conformational change required for MLPH binding is likely more difficult to achieve in other MyoV isoforms due to the sequence differences in the protein core surrounding the Tyr1596.
source: As proposed previously (Pylypenko et al., 2013), the conformational change required for MLPH binding is likely more difficult to achieve in other MyoV isoforms due to the sequence differences in the protein core surrounding the Tyr1596.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and cited reference.

claim: The MyoVa Arg1528 that stabilizes the MLPH-GTBM by two hydrogen bonds is not conserved in the myosin V isoforms and contributes to the MyoVa binding specificity.
source: Moreover, the MyoVa Arg1528 that stabilizes the MLPH-GTBM by two hydrogen bonds (Figure 4E) is not conserved in the myosin V isoforms and contributes to the MyoVa binding specificity (Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural analysis shown in Figure 4E and cited reference.

claim: The observed differences in how Spir-2-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM bind to MyoV-GTD account for their discrepancy in binding specificity.
source: The observed differences in how Spir-2-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM bind to MyoV-GTD thus account for their discrepancy in binding specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis.

claim: The globular tail domain of MyoV binds different partners using the same binding site.
source: The globular tail domain of MyoV thus binds different partners using the same binding site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis showing that Spir and MLPH bind to overlapping sites.

claim: Spir-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM have a similar distribution of charged residues along the sequence.
source: Interestingly, Spir-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM have a similar distribution of charged residues along the sequence: their N-terminal part is positively charged, and their C-terminal sequence, after the specific binding motif, contains a cluster of negatively charged residues (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Spir-2-GTBM binding to MyoV likely uses the charge complementarity described for MLPH-GTBM binding to MyoVa.
source: Thus, Spir-2-GTBM binding to MyoV also likely use the charge complementarity described for MLPH-GTBM binding to MyoVa (Pylypenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed charge distribution similarity and cited reference.

claim: The crystal structure of Rab11a bound to the MyoVa-GTD confirms that Rab11a binds to the MyoVa-GTD SD-2.
source: To gain insights into the relationship between Spir, MyoV and Rab11, we solved the crystal structure of Rab11a bound to the MyoVa-GTD. This structure confirms that Rab11a binds to the MyoVa-GTD SD-2, as previously reported for the MyoVb:Rab11a complex structure (Pylypenko et al., 2013)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure and comparison with previous structures.

claim: Some structural variability in Rab11a occurs upon its binding to the MyoV isoforms.
source: This structure confirms that Rab11a binds to the MyoVa-GTD SD-2, as previously reported for the MyoVb:Rab11a complex structure (Pylypenko et al., 2013) and indicates that some structural variability in Rab11a occurs upon its binding to the MyoV isoforms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Rab11 and Spir binding sites are on opposite ends of the elongated MyoV-GTD.
source: The structures of MyoVa:Spir-GTBM and MyoVa:Rab11a demonstrate that the Rab11 and Spir binding sites are on opposite ends of the elongated MyoV-GTD while the GTD adopts a similar conformation in the two binary complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structures and their comparison.

claim: The two MyoV partners (Rab11 and Spir) can bind to the GTD at the same time.
source: This implies that the two MyoV partners can bind to the GTD at the same time, as shown in a model of the tripartite complex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and supported by the model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The organization of the tripartite complex, where MyoV links Spir to Rab11, provides an explanation of how Spir proteins can be specifically targeted to Rab11 vesicles.
source: The organization of the tripartite complex, where MyoV links Spir to Rab11, provides an explanation of how Spir proteins can be specifically targeted to Rab11 vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Bacterially expressed constitutively active GST-Rab11a-Q70L pulls down transiently over-expressed full-length MyoVa, Spir-2 and a C-terminal FMN2 protein from HEK293 lysates.
source: First, we showed that bacterially expressed constitutively active GST-Rab11a-Q70L pulls down transiently over-expressed full-length MyoVa, Spir-2 and a C-terminal FMN2 protein (mStrawberry-FMN2-FH2-FSI) from HEK293 lysates (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GST-pulldown experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Over-expressed MyoVa-Q1753R mutant impaired in Rab11 binding affects all three proteins co-precipitation with the GST-Rab11a-Q70L-beads.
source: over-expressed MyoVa-Q1753R mutant impaired in Rab11 binding (Lindsay et al., 2013) affects all three proteins co-precipitation with the GST-Rab11a-Q70L-beads consistent with the role of MyoV for linking the MyoV:Spir:FMN2 complex to Rab11.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GST-pulldown experiment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the absence of the MyoVa-GTD, Spir does not pull down Rab11a-Q70L.
source: GST-pulldown experiments with recombinant proteins using GST-Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE also confirm that MyoV serves as a linker between Spir and Rab11. In the absence of the MyoVa-GTD, Spir does not pull down Rab11a-Q70L (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GST-pulldown experiment shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The tripartite complex formation was supported by analytical gel filtration experiments showing co-elution of all three proteins (Rab11a-Q70L, MyoVa-GTD, mCherry-Spir-2-linker).
source: The tripartite complex formation was further supported by analytical gel filtration experiments showing co-elution of all three proteins (Rab11a-Q70L, MyoVa-GTD, mCherry-Spir-2-linker) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analytical gel filtration experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fluorescence microscopy revealed that the three proteins (Myc-Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE, eGFP-MyoVa-CC-GTD, mStrawberry-Rab11a) have a nearly perfect colocalization when transiently co-expressed in HeLa cells.
source: Fluorescence microscopy of immunostained (Myc-Spir-2-GTBM-SB-FYVE) and fluorescent proteins (eGFP-MyoVa-CC-GTD, mStrawberry-Rab11a) revealed that the three proteins have a nearly perfect colocalization when transiently co-expressed in HeLa cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The strong colocalization of Spir and Rab11 was dependent on the Spir MyoV binding motif.
source: The strong colocalization of Spir and Rab11 was dependent on the Spir MyoV binding motif. The Spir-2-SB-FYVE fragment, that lacks the MyoV binding motif, showed membrane localization driven by the FYVE domain (Tittel et al., 2015). When co-expressed with Rab11a and the MyoVa-CC-GTD, a significant reduction in Spir-2-SB-FYVE colocalization with Rab11 was observed, while colocalization of Rab11 with MyoVa-CC-GTD remained high (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: MyoV acts as an adapter to target Spir actin nucleators specifically towards Rab11 vesicle membranes.
source: These data strongly support that MyoV acts as an adapter to target Spir actin nucleators specifically towards Rab11 vesicle membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the colocalization and biochemical data.

claim: MLPH-GTBM binding to the MyoVa-GTD promotes a structural rearrangement in myosin Va in vitro whereby it switches from an inhibited 'OFF' conformation to an extended active 'ON' conformation.
source: MLPH-GTBM binding to the MyoVa-GTD promotes a structural rearrangement in myosin Va in vitro whereby it switches from an inhibited 'OFF' conformation (Figure 6A,B) in which the GTD folds back and binds to the motor domain, to an extended active 'ON' conformation (Yao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The Spir and MLPH binding site overlaps with the MyoVb-GTD N-terminal linker interaction site that has been proposed to contribute to the MyoV OFF state stabilization.
source: Interestingly, the Spir and MLPH binding site also overlaps with the MyoVb-GTD N-terminal linker interaction site that has been proposed to contribute to the MyoV OFF state stabilization (Pylypenko et al., 2013) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural comparison shown in Figure 6A and cited reference.

claim: Spir could play a role in MyoV activation by disrupting the head-tail interaction and opening of the motor.
source: The obvious structural similarity between Spir-GTBM and MLPH-GTBM binding to the MyoVa-GTD suggests that Spir could similarly play a role in MyoV activation by disrupting the head-tail interaction and opening of the motor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity between Spir and MLPH binding.

claim: Full-length MyoVa transiently expressed in cells has an even cytoplasmic distribution.
source: Full-length MyoVa transiently expressed in cells has an even cytoplasmic distribution (Figure 6C) (Lindsay et al., 2013), indicating that the endogenous Rab11 binding activity by itself is not sufficient to target the inhibited motor protein to vesicle membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6C and cited reference.

claim: The endogenous Rab11 binding activity by itself is not sufficient to target the inhibited motor protein to vesicle membranes.
source: Full-length MyoVa transiently expressed in cells has an even cytoplasmic distribution (Figure 6C) (Lindsay et al., 2013), indicating that the endogenous Rab11 binding activity by itself is not sufficient to target the inhibited motor protein to vesicle membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that full-length MyoVa is cytoplasmic despite the presence of endogenous Rab11.

claim: When expressed alone, the N-terminal Spir-2 proteins (Spir-2-KIND-WH2; Spir-2-KIND-WH2-GTBM) have an even cytoplasmic and nuclear localization.
source: When expressed alone, the N-terminal Spir-2 proteins (Spir-2-KIND-WH2; Spir-2-KIND-WH2-GTBM) have an even cytoplasmic and nuclear localization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Co-expressed MyoVa and the N-terminal Spir-2 lacking the GTBM (Myc-Spir-2-KIND-WH2) are both cytosolic.
source: Co-expressed MyoVa and the N-terminal Spir-2 lacking the GTBM (Myc-Spir-2-KIND-WH2) are also both cytosolic (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When full-length MyoVa is co-expressed with a Spir-2 fragment containing the Spir-GTBM (Myc-Spir-2-KIND-WH2-GTBM), both proteins localize to vesicle membranes.
source: In contrast, when full-length MyoVa is co-expressed with a Spir-2 fragment containing the Spir-GTBM (Myc-Spir-2-KIND-WH2-GTBM), both proteins localize to vesicle membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Spir-GTBM binding to cytosolic MyoV activates the motor and promotes its membrane recruitment.
source: This is consistent with a model in which Spir-GTBM binding to cytosolic MyoV activates the motor and promotes its membrane recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MyoVa localizes to vesicles when co-expressed with Spir-GTBM.

claim: The vesicular localization of the full-length MyoVa triggered by Spir-2-GTBM binding was Rab11 dependent.
source: The vesicular localization of the full-length MyoVa triggered by Spir-2-GTBM binding was Rab11 dependent, since a MyoVa point mutant that cannot interact with Rab11 (MyoVa-Q1753R) (Lindsay et al., 2013) fails to be targeted to vesicle membranes and shows an even cytoplasmic distribution, when co-expressed with the Spir-2-KIND-WH2-GTBM protein (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The experiments demonstrate a Rab11-dependent coordinated membrane targeting mechanism of Spir and MyoV.
source: The experiments demonstrate a Rab11-dependent coordinated membrane targeting mechanism of Spir and MyoV (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The timing and mechanism of motor recruitment to specific vesicles is vital for cellular function and its intracellular organization.
source: The timing and mechanism of motor recruitment to specific vesicles is vital for cellular function and its intracellular organization.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of the research topic.

claim: Targeted recruitment of either dynein, kinesins or myosins to vesicles is the essential first step in sorting intracellular cargo within cells.
source: Targeted recruitment of either dynein, kinesins or myosins to vesicles is the essential first step in sorting intracellular cargo within cells yet the logistics of motor activation and vesicle localization are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of motor recruitment.

claim: Rab11 GTPases recruit several different molecular motors to vesicles, regulating trafficking of exocytic and recycling vesicles along microtubule and actin tracks.
source: Rab11 GTPases recruit several different molecular motors to vesicles, regulating trafficking of exocytic and recycling vesicles along microtubule and actin tracks (Welz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The actin nucleator Spir is present on the surface of Rab11-vesicles, enabling them to generate their own tracks for transport by MyoV.
source: The actin nucleator Spir is also present on the surface of Rab11-vesicles, enabling them to generate their own tracks for transport by MyoV (Schuh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The full-length MyoV motor is maintained in a folded, autoinhibited OFF state by an interaction between the N-terminal motor domain and the C-terminal GTD.
source: The full-length MyoV motor is maintained in a folded, autoinhibited OFF state by an interaction between the N-terminal motor domain and the C-terminal GTD. Relief of this interaction by cargo or calcium binding abrogates head-tail binding, resulting in an extended, activated motor (Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2006; Thirumurugan et al., 2006) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Relief of the head-tail interaction by cargo or calcium binding abrogates head-tail binding, resulting in an extended, activated motor.
source: Relief of this interaction by cargo or calcium binding abrogates head-tail binding, resulting in an extended, activated motor (Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2006; Thirumurugan et al., 2006) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: The MyoV motor domain and Rab11 compete for binding to the GTD since the surfaces involved in these interactions are in part overlapping.
source: The MyoV motor domain and Rab11 compete for binding to the GTD since the surfaces involved in these interactions are in part overlapping (namely the H11- H12 loop; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The membrane-anchored Rab11 GTPase alone is not sufficient to target the cytosolic inhibited MyoV to Rab11 positive vesicles in vivo.
source: This explains why the membrane-anchored Rab11 GTPase alone is not sufficient to target the cytosolic inhibited MyoV to Rab11 positive vesicles in vivo (Lindsay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and cited reference.

claim: A drastic change in the localization of MyoV, from cytosol to membranes, occurs when the cellular concentration of Spir-GTBM is increased.
source: However, a drastic change in the localization of MyoV, from cytosol to membranes, occurs when the cellular concentration of Spir-GTBM is increased (Figure 6D) strongly implicating Spir in the recruitment and activation of MyoV on Rab11 vesicles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluorescence microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Spir-GTBM interacts with the same binding pocket in the MyoV-GTD SD-1 that can also be occupied by a short N-terminal linker preceding the MyoV-GTD implicated in stabilizing the OFF state of the myosin.
source: The Spir-GTBM interacts with the same binding pocket in the MyoV-GTD SD-1 (Figure 6A) that can also be occupied by a short N-terminal linker preceding the MyoV-GTD implicated in stabilizing the OFF state of the myosin (Pylypenko et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural analysis shown in Figure 6A and cited references.

claim: Binding of the Spir-GTBM would displace the N-terminal linker and contribute to MyoV activation.
source: Binding of the Spir-GTBM would displace the N-terminal linker and contribute to MyoV activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing overlapping binding sites.

claim: MyoV activation is predicted to involve a competition between inter-GTDs stabilizing interactions within the motor OFF state and Spir binding to SD-1.
source: MyoV activation is thus predicted to involve a competition between inter-GTDs stabilizing interactions within the motor OFF state and Spir binding to SD-1.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: MLPH could activate MyoV in a manner similar to Spir.
source: The Spir and MLPH GTBMs share an overlapping binding site, suggesting that MLPH could activate MyoV in a manner similar to Spir.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity between Spir and MLPH binding.

claim: The Spir/MLPH binding site likely represents a MyoV activation hot spot.
source: Thus, the Spir/MLPH binding site likely represents a MyoV activation hot spot.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both Spir and MLPH can activate MyoV by binding to the same site.

claim: Spir proteins are predicted to exist in a folded state in the cytoplasm.
source: Spir proteins are also predicted to exist in a folded state in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Promiscuous binding of the Spir-FYVE to negatively charged phospholipids is thought to promote an open conformation of the protein.
source: Promiscuous binding of the Spir-FYVE to negatively charged phospholipids is thought to promote an open conformation of the protein (Tittel et al., 2015), facilitating formin recruitment and assembly of an active Spir:FMN complex that promotes actin nucleation on vesicles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The vesicle-bound Spir and Rab11 could synergistically activate and recruit MyoV.
source: Together, the vesicle-bound Spir and Rab11 could then synergistically activate and recruit MyoV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that both Spir and Rab11 contribute to MyoV recruitment.

claim: The resulting membrane bound tripartite complex coordinates nucleation of F-actin tracks and myosin force generation on a subset of Rab11 vesicles.
source: The resulting membrane bound tripartite complex then coordinates nucleation of F-actin tracks and myosin force generation on a subset of Rab11 vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The tripartite complex enables MyoV-driven motility in regions of the cell distal from the cortical actin network, such as in the oocyte cytoplasm.
source: This enables MyoV-driven motility in regions of the cell distal from the cortical actin network, such as in the oocyte cytoplasm (Schuh, 2011) and most likely in the central region of somatic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and cited reference.

claim: The newly synthesized actin filaments emanating from vesicles would favor MyoV-dependent motility as this myosin has been found to have both an increased landing rate and run lengths on ADP-Pi actin filaments.
source: The newly synthesized actin filaments emanating from vesicles would also favor MyoV-dependent motility as this myosin has been found to have both an increased landing rate and run lengths on ADP-Pi actin filaments (Zimmermann et al., 2015) and facilitate actomyosin mediated transport of vesicles towards microtubule tracks (Dietrich et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Different splice forms and variants of Spir and MyoV are implicated in a wide range of cellular functions.
source: Different splice forms and variants of Spir and MyoV are implicated in a wide range of cellular functions, and MyoV interacts with an array of Rab GTPases with roles in a range of transport processes (e.g. Rab3, Rab8 and Rab 32; [Bultema et al., 2014; Lindsay et al., 2013; Roland et al., 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: Spir:MyoV complexes might be recruited via Spir and Rab membrane interactions to a number of different membrane compartments for transport along their own self-generated local actin network.
source: This suggests the possibility that Spir:MyoV complexes might be recruited via Spir and Rab membrane interactions to a number of different membrane compartments for transport along their own self-generated local actin network.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: A splice form of Spir-1 (Spire1C) is specifically localized to the mitochondria.
source: For example, a splice form of Spir-1 (Spire1C) is specifically localized to the mitochondria (Manor et al., 2015) and it is tempting to speculate that it plays a role in recruiting MyoV that has been implicated in regulating the trafficking of this organelle (Pathak et al., 2010; Schwarz, 2013; Sheng, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: MyoV has been implicated in regulating the trafficking of mitochondria.
source: For example, a splice form of Spir-1 (Spire1C) is specifically localized to the mitochondria (Manor et al., 2015) and it is tempting to speculate that it plays a role in recruiting MyoV that has been implicated in regulating the trafficking of this organelle (Pathak et al., 2010; Schwarz, 2013; Sheng, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited references.

claim: A class I myosin recruits the Arp2/3 actin nucleator complex to membranes during endocytic vesicle formation.
source: Interestingly, it has previously been shown that a class I myosin recruits the Arp2/3 actin nucleator complex to membranes during endocytic vesicle formation (Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Coordination of actin nucleation and myosin motors is likely to be a general strategy used by cells to promote myosin dependent motility of membranes.
source: Together with the identification here of a tripartite Spir:MyoV:Rab11 complex that recruits formins to membranes, coordination of actin nucleation and myosin motors is likely to be a general strategy used by cells to promote myosin dependent motility of membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the manuscript and comparison with other systems.
